headlines.article_text: Apple outage follows Microsoft, FAA and JPMorgan disruptions Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Over four days, outages disrupted Microsoft services, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase transactions and Apple. Security researchers say AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, increasing pressure on organizations to patch systems quickly. "When Microsoft goes down, the whole world comes to a standstill," said Raj Rajamani, CEO of JetStream Security. In this article MSFT AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:25 06:25 DNI Jay Clayton: This is not a cyber attack and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state Closing Bell Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton dismissed suspicions that malicious activity led to a series of outages at major tech firms and government agencies over the past week. "This is not cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state," he told CNBC's "Closing Bell" on Tuesday. "We've looked very closely." It's been a tough few days for the technology world after a series of widespread disruptions brought different parts of life to a halt. On Tuesday, an outage halted internal communications at the National Security Agency, and iPhone maker Apple confirmed that different products were either down or having issues . The NSA pointed to "scheduled routine maintenance," while Apple cited "an internal update" as the reason behind its issues. It marked four major system problems in four consecutive business days. watch now VIDEO 2:13 02:13 Apple: Many of our systems back up and running after an internal update caused some outages Power Lunch Microsoft 's Outlook issues wreaked havoc on businesses on Thursday, and the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights on Friday. On Monday, issues at JPMorgan Chase affected customer transactions, and an outage at United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights. "When Microsoft goes down, the whole world comes to a standstill," said Raj Rajamani, CEO of JetStream Security. "That's a stark reminder of how deeply embedded these services and technologies are in our day-to-day life." The disruptions have rattled consumers and led to a steady stream of memes on social media, as people look for a silver lining — or sinister plot — in the string of technology problems. Experts say the real culprit behind this strange series of coincidences is much more benign. "We're in the weird teenage phase of technology not quite maturing enough to know how to do this without disrupting services and so forth," said Tom Hegel, research head at SentinelOne. That's leaving information technology and security teams strained and scrambling to keep up with heightened demand, said Sam Rubin, senior vice president of consulting and threat intelligence at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42. Amid this prolonged period of uncertainty, Rubin said businesses should prioritize updating their most exploitable systems and keeping operations underway when an outage hits. "You need to think about how you continue to operate in the face of one of your IT systems going down," he said. Clayton told CNBC that routine upgrades are commonplace at any organization and called for a nationwide digital infrastructure upgrade. Last week, millions of users lost access to email in a fiasco that Microsoft eventually said was the result of an undetected bug that was lurking since July. The FAA, which is still looking into the root cause of its system failure, pointed in part to a router upgrade in southern Arkansas overseen by government contractor L3Harris Technologies that overwhelmed the agency's telecommunications network. JPMorgan said longer-than-usual service times on Monday stemmed from a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. Agencies and businesses have ruled out cyberattacks, but the routine patching alibi hasn't satisfied some skeptics, and lawmakers are calling for more transparency. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., on Tuesday used the recent incidents to make the case for an AI safety bill. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., acknowledged that it's "too premature" to conclude malicious activity but called for a congressional briefing. "I think it's time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken and we can inform the people of the United States of America," he said during a press conference on Tuesday. watch now VIDEO 3:41 03:41 NSA says it experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance Power Lunch Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news.

headlines.article_text: Skydance names film chiefs for Paramount, Warner Bros labels Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article SKYD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT David Ellison, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., left, and Ynon Kreiz, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., right, at the New York Stock Exchange, Oct. 8, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images Skydance named Don Granger and Kira Goldberg presidents of the Motion Picture Group at Paramount Pictures, while promoting Jesse Ehrman to president of the Motion Picture Group at Warner Bros Pictures, outlining the leadership structure for its combined film business . The changes come as Skydance seeks to build a company capable of delivering 30 films a year, with Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros Pictures retaining separate identities and distinct creative mandates, according to an internal memo to staff on Tuesday from Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein. Kira Goldberg, who joins from Netflix, brings experience overseeing a slate that included the Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence-starrer "Don't Look Up." Josh Goldstine has been named president of worldwide marketing and distribution, overseeing the function across both studios. The restructuring also includes the departure of Ted Lim, Skydance's chief business officer, and Bill Damaschke, who will exit Warner Bros Pictures Animation, according to the memo. Jeff Goldstein, a 48-year veteran of Warner Bros Pictures, will retire and move into a consulting role. At DC Studios, Jeremy Latcham is joining as president and chief creative officer, as previously announced. James Gunn and Peter Safran will step away from their leadership roles and return to full-time creative work, the memo said. (Nasdaq: SLS) (“SELLAS” or the “Company”), a late-stage clinical biopharmaceutical company focused on the development of novel therapies for a broad range of cancer indications, today announced that it has commenced an underwritten public offering of $150.0 million of shares of its common stock. SELLAS intends to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional $22.5 million of shares of its common stock under the same terms and conditions. All of the shares in the offering will be sold by SELLAS. The offering is subject to market and other conditions, and there can be no assurance as to whether or when the offering may be completed, or as to the actual size or terms of the offering.
